papers.title: Verifier-Based Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of Reasoning Models for Thermal Energy Storage Control
papers.abstract: Buildings are expected to shift cooling loads in response to grid conditions. Thermal energy storage (TES) enables this shift, but scheduling it well requires planning hours ahead under storage constraints. Model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning are difficult to scale across buildings. This study instead adapts an open-weight reasoning model through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We convert exact offline dynamic-programming (DP) action values into dense rewards for every candidate action. Using only 30 training prompts, reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) trains the model as an upper-level scheduler that outputs hourly heat-pump setpoints from text-based states and forecasts. Evaluation uses a deliberately simple office-building TES benchmark where exact DP is tractable and the optimum is known. RFT reduces the open-weight model's emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, close to the DP optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2. GPT-5 nearly matches DP and MPC without task-specific training, while GPT-4o, a non-reasoning LLM, produces higher emissions than the no-storage baseline, so inference-time reasoning appears important. Trace analysis shows that RFT mainly stabilizes observable planning patterns (candidate comparison, look-ahead, and feasibility checking) rather than creating a new strategy. Robustness and generalization tests clarify what transfers: the reinforced planning patterns persist under forecast errors and an unseen TES condition and carry over to a battery task, but its different structure limits the gains. DP-based verifiable rewards offer a practical way to adapt open-weight reasoning models to building storage scheduling. These results motivate higher-fidelity tests of whole-building control and scalable verifiers for city-scale energy management.

summary.takeaway: Reinforcement fine-tuning with dynamic programming-based verifiable rewards effectively adapts open-weight reasoning models for thermal energy storage scheduling, achieving near-optimal emissions reduction.
summary.problem: Efficiently scheduling thermal energy storage in buildings requires scalable planning under storage constraints, which is challenging for model predictive control and reinforcement learning methods.
summary.method: The study uses reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards derived from exact offline dynamic programming action values to fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model as an upper-level scheduler.
summary.evidence: Reinforcement fine-tuning reduces emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, closely approaching the dynamic programming optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2 on a simple TES benchmark.
summary.limitations: The approach’s gains are limited when transferring to structurally different tasks like battery control, and higher-fidelity tests on whole-building control remain to be conducted.
summary.why_for_you: This work demonstrates a practical method to leverage verifiable rewards for efficient adversarial training of reasoning LLMs in energy management, relevant for trustworthy and scalable LLM control applications.

signals.text: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) stabilizes planning patterns such as candidate comparison, look-ahead, and feasibility checking rather than inventing new strategies, indicating the model learns to reliably execute known reasoning steps.

The method converts exact offline dynamic programming (DP) action values into dense, verifiable rewards for every candidate action, enabling precise reinforcement learning signal without requiring extensive training data.

Evaluation on a simple office-building TES benchmark shows RFT reduces emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, nearly matching the DP optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2, while GPT-4o without reasoning produces worse emissions than no storage.

papers.title: Show Me How You Reason and I'll Tell You Who You Are: Reasoning Graphs for Robust LLM Authorship Attribution
papers.abstract: Given the current trend to employ large language models (LLMs) in almost any imaginable context, LLM-generated text detection and authorship attribution have become a pressing issue. Prior work has primarily focused on surface-level linguistic features, an approach shown to be susceptible to paraphrasing and other obfuscation techniques. In this paper, we go beyond the linguistic surface, extracting and analysing reasoning structures in LLM-generated texts with the goal of capturing more complex signals of LLM authorship. We propose a graph neural network approach that leverages reasoning graphs extracted by an argument mining pipeline, demonstrating improved robustness and generalisation over a traditional Longformer baseline. Our approach outperforms the baseline by up to 27 percentage points under the obfuscation attacks such as paraphrasing and backtranslation, and 19 percentage points when evaluated on the texts generated by the unseen model versions, simulating real-world conditions in which new LLM versions are continuously released.

summary.takeaway: Reasoning graph-based authorship attribution using graph neural networks significantly improves robustness and generalisation over text-only baselines for LLM-generated texts under obfuscation and unseen model versions.
summary.problem: Existing LLM authorship attribution methods relying on surface-level linguistic features are vulnerable to paraphrasing and fail to generalise across different model versions.
summary.method: The paper proposes a graph neural network approach leveraging reasoning graphs extracted via an argument mining pipeline to capture structural reasoning features for authorship attribution.
summary.evidence: The reasoning graph-based approach outperforms a Longformer baseline by up to 27 percentage points in F1-score under paraphrasing and backtranslation obfuscations and by 19 points when tested on unseen LLM versions.
summary.limitations: The approach does not employ word-level or character-level perturbations, which may limit evaluation of robustness against finer-grained obfuscations.
summary.why_for_you: This method offers a novel, structurally grounded technique to enhance trustworthy LLM authorship attribution, addressing robustness and generalisation challenges critical for reliable AI-generated text identification.

signals.text: The reasoning graph-based fingerprinting approach achieves up to +27% F1-score improvement over text-only baselines under obfuscation attacks such as paraphrasing and backtranslation, demonstrating superior robustness.

The method constructs reasoning graphs from argumentative essays using the oAMF argument mining pipeline and trains graph neural networks (GCN, GAT, Graph Transformer, GPS) to classify LLM authorship.

Paraphrasing via DIPPER and backtranslation through French and Turkish languages introduce lexical and syntactic variation that reduces lexical diversity and essay length, challenging surface-level detection methods.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge of attributing authorship to texts generated by large language models (LLMs), focusing on robustness to obfuscation and generalisation across unseen model versions. Prior methods relying on surface-level linguistic features are vulnerable to paraphrasing and fail to generalise across evolving LLMs. To overcome this, the authors propose a novel approach that extracts reasoning graphs from argumentative essays using an argument mining pipeline, capturing meta-linguistic and pragmatic structures beyond lexical content. These graphs serve as input to various graph neural network architectures, which learn to classify the originating LLM model. The approach is evaluated on a newly created corpus of 2,240 essays from four LLM families and multiple versions, with obfuscation strategies including paraphrasing and backtranslation. Results show substantial improvements in F1-score over a Longformer baseline, with up to 27 percentage points gain under obfuscation and 19 points gain in cross-version generalisation, demonstrating the effectiveness of structural reasoning features for robust authorship attribution.

methodology.title: Reasoning Graph Construction
methodology.detail: Argument mining pipeline (oAMF) extracts argumentative components and relations from essays, representing sentences as nodes with sentence embeddings and edges as argument relations, forming reasoning graphs that capture the text's structural reasoning.

methodology.title: Graph Neural Network Architectures
methodology.detail: Four GNN variants—Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN), Graph Attention Networks (GAT), Graph Transformer, and General Powerful Scalable (GPS) networks—are trained on reasoning graphs to classify LLM authorship, differing in neighborhood aggregation and attention mechanisms.

methodology.title: Node and Edge Encoding
methodology.detail: Nodes are encoded using sentence-transformer embeddings (all-mpnet-base-v2), while edges are processed via argmax or probability distributions over argument relation classes from the ARIR module, enabling relational reasoning in the graph.

methodology.title: Training and Evaluation Setup
methodology.detail: Models are trained and evaluated on the LLM-OWL-AE corpus with two splits: SAME-VERSION (train/test on same model version) and CROSS-VERSION (train/test on different versions), using 200 essays per model for training and 80 for testing, assessing robustness and generalisation.

methodology.title: Authorship Obfuscation Strategies
methodology.detail: Paraphrasing is applied using the DIPPER tool at paragraph level, and backtranslation is performed via French and Turkish using OPUS-MT models, introducing lexical and syntactic variation to test model robustness.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism or Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide formal equations or detailed causal mechanisms but relies on the hypothesis that reasoning graph structures capture meta-linguistic features less affected by surface-level obfuscations, enabling robust authorship attribution.

experiments.title: Dataset and Splits
experiments.detail: The LLM-OWL-AE corpus contains 2,240 argumentative essays from four LLM families and two versions each, with train/test splits for SAME-VERSION and CROSS-VERSION evaluation to test robustness and generalisation.

experiments.title: Baseline and Models
experiments.detail: A Longformer-based text-only baseline is compared against four GNN architectures trained on reasoning graphs, evaluating F1-score performance under original, paraphrased, and backtranslated conditions.

experiments.title: Obfuscation Techniques
experiments.detail: Paraphrasing via DIPPER and backtranslation through French and Turkish are applied to test the models' robustness to lexical and syntactic perturbations that preserve semantic meaning but alter surface features.

experiments.title: Cross-Version Generalisation
experiments.detail: Models trained on earlier LLM versions are tested on later versions and vice versa to assess the ability to generalise authorship attribution across evolving model releases.

findings.title: Robustness to Obfuscation
findings.detail: The reasoning graph-based approach improves F1-score by up to 27 percentage points over the Longformer baseline under paraphrasing and backtranslation obfuscations, demonstrating superior robustness.

findings.title: Generalisation Across Versions
findings.detail: When evaluated on unseen LLM versions, the graph-based method outperforms the baseline by 19 percentage points in F1-score, indicating better generalisation to new model releases.

findings.title: Lexical Diversity Impact
findings.detail: Paraphrasing reduces lexical diversity more severely than backtranslation, with MTLD scores dropping by up to 90 points for some models, challenging surface-level detection but less affecting reasoning graph features.

findings.title: GNN Architecture Performance
findings.detail: Among GNNs, architectures combining local message passing with global attention (GPS) and Graph Transformer variants effectively leverage reasoning graphs for authorship classification.

contributions: Creation and public release of a new dataset of LLM-generated argumentative essays across multiple model versions and families with obfuscation strategies for robustness and generalisation evaluation.
Proposal of a novel reasoning graph-based authorship attribution approach combining language and reasoning features via graph neural networks.
Demonstration of significant performance gains in robustness to obfuscation and generalisation across unseen LLM versions compared to text-only baselines.
limitations: The approach excludes word-level and character-level perturbations, limiting evaluation against finer-grained obfuscation attacks.
No explicit formal mechanism or theoretical explanation is provided for why reasoning graphs capture authorship signals more robustly.
Evaluation is limited to argumentative essays, which may not generalise to other text genres or shorter texts.
Computational resource requirements for argument mining and GNN training are non-trivial, potentially limiting scalability.
open_questions: How well does the reasoning graph-based approach perform on non-argumentative or shorter texts generated by LLMs?
Can the method be extended or adapted to resist finer-grained obfuscations such as character-level perturbations or adversarial paraphrasing?
What are the theoretical underpinnings explaining the robustness of reasoning graphs to obfuscation and model version shifts?
How does the approach scale computationally and perform in real-time or large-scale deployment scenarios?

papers.title: Can LLMs Write Reliable Rubrics? A Meta-Evaluation for Experiment Reproduction
papers.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation is a promising approach for assessing open-ended outputs from LLM-based research agents, particularly in paper reproduction, where direct paper-to-repository comparison is prone to hallucination. However, constructing paper-specific rubrics requires substantial expert effort, limiting the scalability of benchmarks such as PaperBench. In this work, we present, to our knowledge, the first systematic meta-evaluation of LLM-generated rubrics for paper reproduction. We reformulate rubrics into a checklist-style format and evaluate four generation settings across two backbone models. We meta-evaluate generated rubrics intrinsically by semantic similarity and extrinsically by score alignment with ground-truth rubrics. Our results show that the augmented settings substantially improves downstream evaluation alignment, with the strongest setting approaching the human baseline, while intrinsic gains are more modest. Further analyses reveal that LLM-generated rubrics are often overly fine-grained, biased toward high scores, and less adaptive to paper domains, highlighting both the affordances and limitations.

summary.takeaway: Augmented LLM-generated rubrics substantially improve alignment with human evaluation in paper reproduction tasks, nearing human baseline performance.
summary.problem: Constructing paper-specific rubrics for evaluating LLM-based paper reproduction is expert-intensive and limits benchmark scalability.
summary.method: The study meta-evaluates LLM-generated rubrics reformulated into checklist format across four generation settings and two backbone models using intrinsic semantic similarity and extrinsic score alignment.
summary.evidence: Augmented rubric generation settings show substantial improvement in downstream evaluation alignment, with the best setting approaching human baseline, despite modest intrinsic semantic gains.
summary.limitations: LLM-generated rubrics tend to be overly fine-grained, biased toward high scores, and less adaptive to diverse paper domains.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides critical insights into automating rubric generation for trustworthy evaluation of LLM research agents, addressing hallucination-prone direct comparisons.

signals.text: The strongest augmented rubric generation setting achieves downstream evaluation alignment close to human baseline, demonstrating effective rubric automation for paper reproduction.
Rubrics are reformulated into a checklist-style format and evaluated across four generation settings and two backbone LLMs, enabling systematic meta-evaluation of rubric quality.
Intrinsic evaluation via semantic similarity shows only modest gains, indicating that semantic closeness alone is insufficient to guarantee evaluation alignment.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the challenge of scalable, reliable evaluation of LLM-generated research outputs in paper reproduction tasks, where direct comparison to repositories is prone to hallucination. The authors propose automating rubric generation using LLMs and conduct the first systematic meta-evaluation of these rubrics. They convert rubrics into checklist-style formats and test four generation settings across two backbone models. Evaluation is twofold: intrinsic semantic similarity and extrinsic score alignment with ground-truth rubrics. Results reveal that augmented rubric generation settings significantly improve downstream evaluation alignment, nearly matching human baselines, while intrinsic semantic similarity gains remain modest. Further analysis uncovers that LLM-generated rubrics are often overly detailed, biased toward higher scores, and less adaptable across paper domains. These findings highlight both the potential and current limitations of LLM-generated rubrics for trustworthy, scalable evaluation in LLM-based research agent benchmarks.

methodology.title: Generation Settings

methodology.title: Backbone Models
methodology.detail: Two backbone LLMs serve as the basis for rubric generation, enabling analysis of model-dependent effects on rubric reliability and adaptability.

methodology.title: Intrinsic Meta-Evaluation
methodology.detail: Generated rubrics are evaluated intrinsically by measuring semantic similarity to ground-truth rubrics, assessing content closeness independent of scoring outcomes.

methodology.title: Extrinsic Meta-Evaluation
methodology.detail: Rubrics are extrinsically evaluated by aligning their scoring outcomes with ground-truth rubric scores, measuring practical evaluation reliability.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal mechanisms but focuses on empirical meta-evaluation of rubric generation and scoring alignment.

experiments.title: Rubric Generation and Evaluation
experiments.detail: Experiments involve generating rubrics under four settings using two backbone LLMs, reformulating rubrics into checklist format, and evaluating via intrinsic semantic similarity and extrinsic score alignment metrics.

findings.title: Augmented Settings Improve Alignment
findings.detail: Augmented rubric generation settings substantially improve downstream evaluation alignment, with the strongest setting approaching human baseline performance.

findings.title: Modest Intrinsic Gains
findings.detail: Intrinsic semantic similarity between generated and ground-truth rubrics shows only modest improvement, indicating semantic closeness is not fully predictive of evaluation quality.

findings.title: Overly Fine-Grained Rubrics
findings.detail: LLM-generated rubrics tend to be overly detailed, which may complicate evaluation and reduce practical usability.

findings.detail: Rubrics generated by LLMs are less adaptive to different paper domains, limiting generalizability across diverse research topics.

Demonstration that augmented rubric generation settings improve downstream evaluation alignment near human baselines.
